ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: No papers appeared to involve live data collection requiring an ethics approval statement.
ethics_check.report: We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Dense, standardized species-by-trait matrices support comparative biology and ecology, but their coverage remains uneven.
LifeDive uses a general-purpose, web-search-enabled language model within a scripted annotation pipeline to estimate traits across animals, plants, and fungi.
The workflow assembled 35,856 species by 196 phenotype questions, yielding 7,027,776 entries in a completed matrix; 16.6% of entries were imputed from other machine-derived annotations.
Four ordered substantive responses express model judgments about trait statements, with a separate code for unknown or inapplicable cases.
An exploratory 14-factor representation summarized broad biological contrasts, although statistical factor-retention criteria suggested substantially more dimensions.
A benchmark screened 168 external criteria, with selected results reported for 44; many biologically direct associations were strong, particularly for taxonomy and selected ecological traits.
A separate model-assisted audit reported 96.5% directional agreement in a selected taxonomy-rule subset and approximately 237 agreements among 240 selected species-specific checks.

These audit subsets do not estimate accuracy across the whole matrix, and the AmphiBIO-derived benchmark results require qualification because unrecorded categories were treated as negative indicators.
Trait profiles also produced recognizable taxonomic and functional groupings.
LifeDive offers a broad computational phenotype resource for exploration, hypothesis generation, and prioritizing expert review.
Individual values remain estimates, and downstream inference requires attention to imputation, sampling, source dependence, and trait-specific verification.
The reported application programming interface and computing expenditure was approximately US$10,000.

text.text: Selected external-criterion associations
The main text distinguishes the completed data product from original annotations.
External correlations are selected associations; the model-assisted audit is a qualified exploratory assessment.
The supplementary tables preserve reported outputs and identify unavailable or coding-sensitive entries.
Phenotypes connect evolutionary history to ecological function.

Morphology, physiology, behavior, life history, habitat use, trophic strategy, stress tolerance and reproductive mode determine how organisms interact with one another and with their environments, and they supply the raw material for comparative biology, macroecology, conservation prioritization and functional biodiversity science.

These fields increasingly depend on large, standardized matrices of organismal characteristics: whether a species is woody, venomous, photosynthetic, aquatic, parasitic, drought-tolerant, long-lived, edible, human-associated or sensitive to pollution.
Yet the underlying data remain uneven.

Landmark trait resources have transformed plant ecology, ornithology and mammalian macroecology, but dense species-by-trait matrices are hard to assemble: expert curation is slow, taxonomic coverage is biased, and missingness is structured by clade, geography, body size, charisma and research effort (Domazetoski et al., 2025; Kattge et al., 2020; Marcos et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Landmark trait resources have transformed plant ecology, ornithology and mammalian macroecology, but dense species-by-trait matrices are hard to assemble: expert curation is slow, taxonomic coverage is biased, and missingness is structured by clade, geography, body size, charisma and research effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Domazetoski et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kattge et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Marcos et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Existing databases show both the value and the constraint.

PanTHERIA, EltonTraits, COMBINE and AVONET made broad comparative analyses possible by harmonizing life-history, ecological, morphological and geographic attributes across mammals or birds while carefully documenting taxonomy, synonymy, missingness and provenance (Jones et al., 2009; Soria et al., 2021; Tobias et al., 2022; Wilman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: PanTHERIA, EltonTraits, COMBINE and AVONET made broad comparative analyses possible by harmonizing life-history, ecological, morphological and geographic attributes across mammals or birds while carefully documenting taxonomy, synonymy, missingness and provenance <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Jones et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Soria et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tobias et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Wilman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Their success also exposes a bottleneck: each new trait domain or clade typically requires renewed expert reading, taxonomic reconciliation and quality control.

Cross-kingdom work is especially demanding, because a useful matrix must place traits as different as cell walls, venom, gills, lignin degradation, seed dispersal and endosymbiosis onto a single response framework.
In such settings, imputation and uncertainty are not peripheral technicalities; they become part of the resource itself.
This constraint binds most tightly at the scales at which macroecology and biogeography operate.

Global analyses of functional diversity, trait-environment relationships, community assembly and extinction risk require trait values for every species in an assemblage, yet the assemblages that matter are rarely confined to one well-curated clade.
A forest plot contains trees, fungi, arthropods and vertebrates; a lake contains macrophytes, invertebrates and fishes.

Analysts therefore either restrict their questions to the clades for which matrices exist, or impute across gaps whose structure is itself biased by the same taxonomic and geographic factors that produced the gaps.

A resource that applies one response framework across kingdoms addresses a different problem from the one solved by any single expert database: it trades trait-specific precision for comparability, so that the same question can be put to a tree, a bird, a fungus, a mollusc and an insect.

Automated text mining can accelerate trait mobilization by converting floras, monographs, web pages, and articles into structured records (Endara et al., 2018; Farrell et al., 2024; Folk et al., 2024).

text.text: Recent large language model (LLM) systems extract ecological records, plant traits, and species interactions from unstructured text (Castro et al., 2024; Gougherty & Clipp, 2024; Keck et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent large language model (LLM) systems extract ecological records, plant traits, and species interactions from unstructured text <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Castro et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gougherty & Clipp, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Keck et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Extraction remains constrained by source access, wording, and controlled vocabularies.

A complementary approach is to ask a model to estimate a trait even when a particular source does not state it explicitly; doing so broadens coverage but changes the evidentiary status of the resulting value from an extracted observation to an inference.

Pretrained language models encode factual and relational information, but they can also produce fluent errors and are sensitive to prompt wording, training distribution, and retrieval context Permanent preprint • November 2026 mooremetrics.com/lifedive (Petroni et al., 2019; Wysocka et al., 2024).

text.text: A computational trait resource therefore needs separate assessments of recognizable structure, external agreement, and the reliability of individual entries.
LifeDive applies one question set across kingdoms and uses a scripted batch workflow to make large-scale annotation feasible for an individual investigator.
The reported API and computing expenditure was approximately US$10,000.
This expenditure describes the present workflow; no matched comparison of labor, cost, or accuracy with expert curation was conducted.
This paper has two aims: to document the annotation and processing workflow, and to assess whether its output preserves recognizable biological structure.
The evidence consists of factor analysis, selected external benchmark associations, a model-assisted audit of subsets of cells from 200 randomly selected species, and a phenotype-similarity network.
These complementary analyses assess internal structure, external agreement, and agreement for selected cells.
Detailed methods, additional results, the audit prompt and an edited account of its findings, and supplementary tables are included in this PDF.
Species candidates came from the Catalogue of Life checklist, version 2026-04-18 XR (Catalogue of Life, 2026).
The compilation retained accepted or provisionally accepted records at species rank, with available higher taxonomy and English vernacular names.
Sampling focused on Animalia, Plantae, and Fungi and included approximately 5% extinct species.
A family-first algorithm aimed to represent every eligible family, then filled the remaining quota from species not already chosen.
Priorities favored fully accepted names, English common names, and Animalia and Plantae over Fungi; a small random component broke ties under a fixed seed.
This procedure returned 35,000 species.

GPT 5.5 Pro was then asked to identify familiar organisms missing from the list, including examples such as the barn owl (Tyto alba) and Brazilian wandering spider (Phoneutria nigriventer), producing the final sample of 35,856.
The sample is designed for breadth and familiarity, rather than as a probability sample of global biodiversity.
The final analysis retained 196 questions spanning cellular biology, anatomy and structure, physiology, behavior, reproduction, life history, ecology, environmental tolerance, and human salience.
Table 1 gives examples; Table S2 preserves the complete retained question wording.

text.text: Responses used four ordered substantive categories: 0, Definitely No; 1, Probably No; 3, Probably Yes; and 4, Definitely Yes.
Code 2 denoted Unknown or not applicable and was not treated as an ordinal midpoint in analysis.
This response format expresses the model's endorsement of a proposition, rather than a common physical quantity or a measured amount of a trait.
The same questions can be applied across kingdoms, but some are ambiguous or biologically inapplicable for particular taxa.

Cellular biology Does this organism produce cellulose?

Phenotype annotations were collected with the xAI Grok Batch application programming interface (xAI, 2026), using the scripted model grok-4-1-fast-reasoning with web search enabled so that the model could retrieve information on obscure taxa.
Batch processing was chosen because the task consisted of many independent species-by-question inference requests.

Species were processed in groups of three; each prompt listed the species and questions, defined the response scale and required a complete comma-separated row for every species, with every cell populated and the Unknown code used where an answer could not be determined.
The scripted workflow validated requests before upload, saved and polled batch identifiers, retrieved completed results with pagination, and checkpointed parsed data.

The parser removed code fences, aligned question columns by identifier, padded or trimmed responses with too few or too many species rows, and converted nonnumeric, missing, or unreliably aligned cells to the Unknown code.
Requests with extraction errors, missing response text, or unreliable column alignment were logged for retry.
These checks address format and alignment; they do not establish biological correctness.
Row padding or trimming also requires reliable identity matching.
The results are computational phenotype estimates, not direct measurements or expert-curated observations.

text.text: Annotation was conducted in 11 question subsets and merged by species.
Unknown/not applicable and out-of-range values were treated as missing.
Columns were retained when they had fewer than 25,000 missing values, leaving 196 analyzed questions.
This permissive item-level threshold is distinct from the overall missing-cell rate of 16.6%.
Missing responses were imputed item by item with multinomial random forests (Breiman, 2001) in H2O version 3.46.0.9 (H2O.ai, 2026).
text.formatted: Missing responses were imputed item by item with multinomial random forests <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Breiman, 2001)</ref> in H2O version 3.46.0.9 (H2O.ai, 2026).

text.text: The model for each item used its observed values as training outcomes and the other retained items as predictors, with a fixed seed and randomized item order.
Predicted classes were inserted only into missing target cells.
The completed matrix was used for the latent-structure analyses.
Original unimputed responses remain the appropriate starting point for interpreting individual annotations.
Imputation predicts a missing response category from other machine-generated categories; it does not create a new biological observation or distinguish an unknown trait from an inapplicable question.
The reported analyses do not separately establish imputation accuracy or propagate imputation uncertainty.
After imputation, the four substantive categories were recoded as 0, 1, 2, and 3, corresponding to original codes 0, 1, 3, and 4.
Exploratory factor analysis of the polychoric correlation matrix was performed with psych::irt.fa, which also expresses resulting parameters in item-response-theory terms (Revelle, 2026).

text.text: The benchmark contained 168 numeric criteria from public trait resources and a standardized taxonomic backbone.

Sources included bird and mammal traits from EltonTraits 1.0 (Wilman et al., 2014), mammal traits from PanTHERIA (Jones et al., 2009) and MammalDIET (Kissling et al., 2014), amphibian traits from AmphiBIO (Oliveira et al., 2017), marine-invertebrate traits from SeaLifeBase (Palomares & Pauly, 2024), fish traits from FishBase (Froese & Pauly, 2024), and taxonomy from the traitdata package and GBIF Backbone Taxonomy ( GBIF Secretariat, 2023; RS-eco, 2023).

text.text: The model assigned broad taxonomic groups and constructed expected answers for approximately 50 questions it judged largely predictable from those groups.
It also assessed 240 selected species-specific cells, spanning 20 species and 12 questions, using its knowledge and targeted web checks.
No independent human expert adjudication was reported.
The two procedures used the same auditing model, and neither the rule-covered questions nor the smaller spot-check sample constituted a uniform random sample of all cells.
Section S3 gives the original prompt, an edited account of the procedures, and the limitations of the reported counts.
For the same 200 species, pairwise phenotype-profile similarity was summarized using polychoric correlations across the 196 questions (Olsson, 1979; Revelle, 2026).

The resulting coefficients are descriptive profile similarities whose interpretation depends on question content, redundancy, shared absences, and the latent-distribution assumptions.
Negative correlations were retained in numerical summaries and set to zero for plotting.

The nonnegative weighted matrix was drawn with qgraph version 1.10.1 using a force-directed spring layout (Epskamp et al., 2012; Fruchterman & Reingold, 1991), with nodes grouped as Arthropoda, Ascomycota, Chordata, Cnidaria, Mollusca, Tracheophyta, or Other.

text.text: The workflow produced a completed matrix of 35,856 species by 196 retained questions, comprising 7,027,776 entries.
Of these entries, 16.6% were filled by statistical imputation after Unknown/not applicable and out-of-range responses were treated as missing.
The retained questions include cellular and structural traits, anatomy, ecological associations, life history, environmental tolerances, and human-associated descriptions.
Human-salience variables, including perceived beauty and nuisance status, are part of the resource but should not be confused with direct organismal measurements.
The 14-factor descriptive solution was interpretable in terms of broad biological profiles (Table 2).
text.formatted: The 14-factor descriptive solution was interpretable in terms of broad biological profiles (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: The reported primary-loading counts were 82 Plant-like, 12 Fungus-like, 19 Aquatic, 15 Insect-like, 5 Simple, 10 Robust, 12 Durable, 10 Bird-like, 5 Dangerous, 5 Shelled, 5 Drought-tolerant, 7 Parasitic, 6 Cold-tolerant, and 3 Environmentally-sensitive items, summing to 196.
The pattern table is selectively displayed and rounded; Table S2 marks three unavailable Bird-like coefficients as NR.
Counts are preserved from the analysis summary rather than reconstructed from the incomplete rounded table.

Fungus-like captured a distinct nonanimal syndrome, comprising lignin-degrading enzymes, siderophores, multinucleate cells, decomposer nutrition, predominantly haploid life stages, filamentous growth and extracellular digestion.

Aquatic loaded on underwater survival, aquatic habitat, gill-like gas exchange, salinity tolerance and indeterminate growth, and negatively on dead-mass shedding, post-fire recovery and thermogenesis, separating aquatic profiles from terrestrial plant regrowth and endothermic animals.

Insect-like loaded on chitin, chitinase, very small body mass, short lifespan and surface gas-exchange openings, and negatively on closed vascular systems, rigid internal skeletons and hemoglobin-like physiology.
These dimensions summarize recognizable cross-kingdom contrasts in the selected question set.
Plant-like was the broadest dimension, contrasting cellulose production, photosynthesis, large vacuoles, and plant-associated chemistry with animal-associated physiology.

The narrower profiles included nuisance and invasiveness under Robust; body size, longevity, and durable structures under Durable; appearance, aerial, and reproductive features under Bird-like; and venom, toxicity, and perceived hazard under Dangerous.
Simple summarized budding, gelatinous tissues, and colonial organization.
These labels describe covariance among the particular questions; they do not measure evolutionary advancement or define mutually exclusive kinds of organisms.
A species can score highly on multiple profiles.

text.text: English oak and coast redwood occupy the high-Plant-like, high-Durable region, whereas sunflower, dandelion, water-lily, and bracken fern remain high on Plant-like but lower on Durable.
Many animals have negative Plant-like scores, while large or structurally robust animals tend to have higher Durable scores than smaller or delicate animals.
Fungal examples occupy an intermediate Plant-like region and generally have low Durable scores.
In the Aquatic-versus-Dangerous panel, many fishes and marine invertebrates have elevated Aquatic scores, and several venomous or predatory species have elevated Dangerous scores.
The great white shark combines both profiles.
The common bottlenose dolphin and humpback whale, however, lie near zero on the standardized Aquatic axis despite being marine mammals.
This illustrates that a factor score summarizes the full pattern of included traits rather than literal habitat membership.
These selected examples aid interpretation; they are not a held-out validation of the dimensions or a quantitative measure of risk to humans.

text.text: Of the 35,856 species, 15,525 (43.3%) matched at least one external resource, with coverage strongest for vertebrates and weaker for plants, fungi, and most invertebrates.
Table 3 presents selected direct correspondences; Table S3 retains all five reported matches for each of 44 selected criteria.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">3</ref> presents selected direct correspondences; Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> retains all five reported matches for each of 44 selected criteria.

text.text: The displayed subset is not a comprehensive summary of all 168 criteria screened.
Broad taxonomic associations were often strong.
Animalia was negatively associated with cellulose production (r = -0.99), cell walls (r = -0.97), and photosynthesis (r = -0.97), and positively associated with centrioles (r = 0.98).
Plantae showed the reverse pattern.
Mammalia was associated with hair, fur, or trichomes (r = 0.99) and negatively associated with the item about seeds, eggs outside the body, or spores (r = -0.98).

Arthropoda and Insecta were associated with chitin (both r = 0.97), and fish-class indicators were associated with gill-like gas exchange (r = 0.96), underwater survival (r = 0.95), and aquatic lifestyle (r = 0.93).
These are contrasts among broad groups, not evidence that every item is accurate within a group.

Selected ecological associations also matched their intended content: bird nocturnality with nighttime activity (r = 0.92), marine-mammal foraging with underwater survival (r = 0.97), marine-invertebrate host association with parasitism (r = 0.89), and marine-invertebrate sessility with the sessile-life item (r = 0.84).
Other large correlations had no clear biological interpretation, including some matches involving lignin degradation within mammals or birds.
Sparse cross-tabulations, source coding, annotation errors, and selecting extrema may all contribute.
Large absolute correlations alone are therefore insufficient evidence of validity.
AmphiBIO-derived associations are not used here as confirmation of biological absences because of the missing-value recoding described above.

text.text: The audit reported 96.5% directional agreement for a taxonomy-rule subset with a final stated denominator of 7,641 cells, and approximately 237 agreements among 240 selected species-specific checks.
The original confidence-stratum counts total 7,643 rather than 7,641; this discrepancy is retained explicitly in the audit summary.
The audited matrix contained no Unknown codes, but that does not establish the raw model's abstention rate because cell-level preprocessing and imputation provenance were not resolved in the report.

These selected, model-adjudicated checks provide exploratory evidence about the examined cells; they do not establish a 95-97% accuracy rate for the complete dataset or calibrated probabilities for individual response codes.
The phenotype-similarity network showed recognizable taxonomic and functional organization (Figure 2).

Examples of strong similarities included pairs of trees, frogs, flatfishes, and sea anemones.
Some cross-group similarities also had plausible functional interpretations, such as an active predatory cuttlefish near fishes.
These patterns describe organization in the generated trait matrix; they do not independently verify its entries.

text.text: LifeDive demonstrates a practical way to assemble a broad computational phenotype matrix across animals, plants, and fungi.
Its 7,027,776 completed entries contain recognizable biological contrasts, and selected external associations agree with established trait resources.
The combination of broad coverage and a common question framework can support exploratory comparisons, hypothesis generation, and prioritization of expert review.
The evidence is strongest for these descriptive uses; it does not establish general cell-level accuracy or predictive performance across all traits and taxa.
The reported expenditure makes the scale of the workflow concrete, but it should not be read as an estimate of the cost of producing an equivalently accurate expert-curated resource.
Likewise, format constraints, retry logic, and web search were components of the workflow rather than experimentally isolated causes of performance.
Web search was enabled, but its contribution was not separately tested.

The roles of schema design, parsing, provenance, and expert verification are consistent with broader work on scientific use of language models (Dagdelen et al., 2024; Farrell et al., 2024; Polak & Morgan, 2024).
text.formatted: The roles of schema design, parsing, provenance, and expert verification are consistent with broader work on scientific use of language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dagdelen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Farrell et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Polak & Morgan, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Users should distinguish raw annotations from completed data.
The raw response categories retain Unknown/not applicable values and are preferable for reviewing individual traits.
The completed matrix is convenient for methods requiring complete input, but its imputed cells are predictions from other machine-generated annotations.
Analyses should preserve the original category and an imputation indicator wherever these are available, and verify influential species-by-trait values against appropriate biological sources.
A definite response is a model judgment, not a guarantee of correctness.
The substantive categories are ordered, but equal spacing between their numerical codes is an analytical assumption.
Aggregate scores depend on the included questions and score-construction rules, and should be named and interpreted as relative profiles.
For example, the Aquatic factor is not a direct habitat classification, Dangerous is not a calibrated risk measure, and Simple does not imply evolutionary primitiveness.
Human-salience items describe model-and source-mediated human judgments.
Their usefulness and potential biases differ from those of anatomical or physiological questions.
The species sample also reflects deliberate selection.
It emphasizes broad family coverage, accepted names, common names, and familiar organisms, with differing priorities among kingdoms.
Analyses of prevalence, diversity, or global biodiversity should not treat it as a representative random draw.
Trait meanings may depend on life stage, sex, location, environmental conditions, or the definition of the organism; the shared question framework does not eliminate these sources of variation.

text.text: Several features can make apparent agreement stronger than generalizable accuracy.
The factor analysis and network summarize the same generated matrix.
Benchmark resources were curated outside this study but were not shown to be absent from the annotation model's training data or web retrieval.
Different language models can share source material and systematic errors.
Taxonomic contrasts may dominate both internal structure and external correlations, while selecting the largest correlations among many candidates favors extreme values.
The 44 reported criteria do not establish performance over the entire benchmark, and some large coefficients are biologically indirect or implausible.
The model-assisted audit is limited by selected questions, selected spot-check species, fallible reference judgments, and unresolved count and preprocessing details.
It cannot supply an overall accuracy estimate without a representative sampling design and independently adjudicated reference labels.
Confidence-stratified agreement in the original report likewise does not establish probabilistic calibration.

A future audit should sample cells across taxa and trait domains, distinguish generated and imputed values, preserve source citations and adjudication decisions, and account for clustering by species and question.
Missingness creates a separate limitation.
Unknown and inapplicable responses were combined before imputation, and imputed entries may strengthen apparent covariance.
The stability of factor structure and scores under alternative missing-data treatments was not established.
Fourteen factors were selected for interpretability despite much larger estimates from the retention criteria.
The present representation is therefore one useful descriptive reduction, not a claim that organismal phenotypes have exactly fourteen underlying dimensions.
Sensitivity analyses should also examine within-clade structure and alternative similarity estimators.
The AmphiBIO recoding illustrates why benchmark provenance matters as much as model output.
An undocumented category cannot automatically be treated as an observed absence.
A corrected analysis should retain uncertainty or establish explicit negatives from suitable source records before estimating presence/absence performance.
The original AmphiBIO correlations are preserved as flagged outputs for transparency, rather than silently relabeled as corrected results.
Reproducibility is best understood at the level of a versioned data product.
The workflow can be rerun, but exact annotations from a commercial model with web retrieval may change with model updates, prompts, API behavior, and source availability.
Reuse should identify the dataset version, model identifier, collection dates, prompt and question versions, processing code, response scale, and validation materials.
Cell-level source and imputation metadata are needed to distinguish generated, predicted, checked, and unchecked entries.
General concerns about factuality, source bias, and responsible open-data practice apply to this resource (Chafetz et al., 2024; Nasr & El-Deeb, 2025; Wysocka et al., 2024).
text.formatted: General concerns about factuality, source bias, and responsible open-data practice apply to this resource <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chafetz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nasr & El-Deeb, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Wysocka et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future development can combine expert adjudication with targeted model annotation.

Priorities include checking influential cells and poorly covered taxa, resolving ambiguous questions, separating unknown from inapplicable responses, verifying taxonomic identity, and correcting benchmark coding.
Cross-model agreement can help triage review but should itself be validated.
Predefined trait-to-criterion mappings, held-out evaluations, and comparison with simple

text.text: A constrained language-model workflow can assemble a cross-kingdom phenotype resource with broad coverage and recognizable biological structure.
LifeDive provides such a resource for 35,856 species, together with descriptive dimensions and exploratory comparisons.
Its principal contribution is a documented computational trait layer and a concrete basis for further evaluation.

The resource is most useful when its estimates, imputation, selective validation, and sampling design remain visible to users and when conclusions that depend on specific traits are checked against biological evidence.

The taxon-selection workflow aimed to represent every eligible family while moderately preferring species with common names.

It used a Catalogue of Life Data Package (ColDP), read NameUsage.tsv, normalized prefixed column names, and retained species-rank records with accepted or provisionally accepted status (Catalogue of Life, 2026).
Taxonomic identifiers and available kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, and genus fields were retained.
Binomials were constructed from genericName and specificEpithet when available, with scientificName as a fallback.
English vernacular names were merged from VernacularName.tsv, using the first English record when several were available.
The representative organism selection focused on Animalia, Plantae, and Fungi, including approximately 5% extinct species.

The script then selected a target set by first choosing the highest-priority species in each family, thereby preserving broad family-level taxonomic coverage, and then filling remaining slots from the highest-priority species not already selected.

The priority score favored fully accepted names over provisionally accepted names, species with an English common name, and Animalia/Plantae over Fungi; a small random component was added only as a tie-breaker, with a fixed random seed for reproducibility.
This resulted in the initial set of 35,000 organisms.
Further inspection of the list revealed that many commonly known organisms (e.g., barn owl, Brazilian wandering spider) were missing.
I therefore asked an LLM (GPT 5.5 Pro) to compile a list of well-known organisms that were not included in the list of 35,000.
This resulted in a final list of 35,856 organisms.
Phenotype annotations were collected with the xAI Grok API using batch processing.
Batch processing was selected because the task consisted of many independent organism-by-question inference requests, a use case for which asynchronous batch APIs are designed (xAI, 2026).
text.formatted: Batch processing was selected because the task consisted of many independent organism-by-question inference requests, a use case for which asynchronous batch APIs are designed <ref type="bibr">(xAI, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the R workflow, API credentials were loaded from an environment file, requests were submitted to the xAI /v1/batches endpoint, and individual inference jobs targeted the /v1/responses endpoint.
The scripted model name was grok-4-1-fast-reasoning, and each request enabled the web_search tool so that the model could use web search for obscure taxa.
Each species was evaluated using substantive response codes0 = Definitely No,1 = Probably No,3 = Probably Yes, and4 = Definitely Yes, with code 2 reserved for Unknown or not applicable.
The final analysis retained 196 phenotype questions.
Names were sanitized for JSON and comma-separated output.
Each request listed three organisms, the current question subset, and the response definitions, and required one row per organism with one numeric column per question.
Every cell was to be populated, using code 2 when an answer could not be determined.
This is a four-category substantive response scale with a separate missing/inapplicable category, rather than a five-level trait-intensity continuum.
The batch workflow included several quality-control steps.
JSONL requests were generated and validated before upload.
After a batch was created, the script saved the batch identifier, polled batch status, resumed from saved identifiers when possible, retrieved completed results using

text.text: The parser stripped code-fence formatting, read the CSV response, aligned question columns using Q-number headers when available, padded or trimmed rows if a response returned too few or too many organism rows, replaced nonnumeric or missing cells with the Unknown code, and logged problematic requests.
Responses with unreliable column shifts were discarded and replaced with Unknown values rather than silently treated as valid data.
A retry JSONL file was generated for requests with extraction errors, missing response text, assignment errors, or unreliable column alignment.
Because the values are model-generated annotations, they should be interpreted as computational phenotype estimates rather than direct measurements or expert-curated observations.
The phenotype collection was conducted in multiple item subsets to avoid overloading individual LLM requests.
The script read 11 organism-by-item CSV matrices, assigned the original phenotype-question text as column names, and merged the subsets by organism.
The Unknown/not applicable response code was then treated as missing.
Values outside the response scale were also set to missing.
Items with very high missingness were excluded by retaining columns with fewer than 25,000 missing values; the retained set was renamed Q1 through Q196 for imputation and subsequent factor analysis.
Missing item responses were imputed using random forest classification, an ensemble method based on aggregating many decision trees (Breiman, 2001).
text.formatted: Missing item responses were imputed using random forest classification, an ensemble method based on aggregating many decision trees <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Breiman, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The imputation code initialized an H2O cluster with 14 threads and iterated through the 196 items in random order with a fixed seed.

For each target item, rows with observed values on that item were used as the training set; the target item was converted to a categorical outcome; all other retained phenotype items were used as predictors; and h2o.randomForest was used to train a multinomial classifier (H2O.ai, 2026).
Predicted classes were then inserted only for cases missing on the target item.
This process yielded a complete organism-by-phenotype matrix for the retained 196 items.
After imputation, original codes 0, 1, 3, and 4 were recoded to 0, 1, 2, and 3.

The matrix was analyzed with psych::irt.fa, which performs exploratory factor analysis of tetrachoric or polychoric correlations and expresses associated parameters in IRT terms (R Core Team, 2026; Revelle, 2026).
A 14-factor solution with promax rotation was selected for interpretability (Fabrigar et al., 1999; Hendrickson & White, 1964).
text.formatted: A 14-factor solution with promax rotation was selected for interpretability <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fabrigar et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hendrickson & White, 1964)</ref>.

text.text: Parallel analysis suggested 58 factors and the minimum-average-partial criterion suggested 41 (Horn, 1965; Velicer, 1976), so 14 should be understood as a descriptive reduction.
text.formatted: Parallel analysis suggested 58 factors and the minimum-average-partial criterion suggested 41 <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Horn, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Velicer, 1976)</ref>, so 14 should be understood as a descriptive reduction.

text.text: Unit-weighted sum scores based on the loading patterns were used instead of theta scores to reduce domination by a small number of highly discriminating items.
The selectively displayed, rounded loading table is insufficient to reproduce every scoring detail; exact item selection, reverse scoring, and transformations require the analysis code.

The 14 score dimensions were labeled on the basis of high-loading items as Plant-like, Fungus-like, Aquatic, Insect-like, Simple, Robust, Durable, Bird-like, Dangerous, Shelled, Drought-tolerant, Parasitic, Cold-tolerant, and Environmentally-sensitive.
The signs of the Parasitic and Cold-tolerant scores were reversed to make higher scores correspond to higher levels of the named construct.
For visualization only, a small uniform random jitter was added to the factor scores to reduce overplotting; the script notes that these jittered scores were not

The validation strategy examined several aspects of the LifeDive resource.

External comparisons assessed agreement with existing resources; a model-assisted audit examined selected cells among 200 randomly sampled species; and factor analysis and network visualization summarized internal structure.
These assessments answer different questions.
In particular, selection of random species does not make the subsequently chosen audit questions or spot-check cells a representative sample of all 7,027,776 entries.
The external benchmark used public trait resources and a taxonomic backbone.
EltonTraits supplies bird and mammal diet, foraging, mass, and activity information (Wilman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: EltonTraits supplies bird and mammal diet, foraging, mass, and activity information <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wilman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Other resources were PanTHERIA (Jones et al., 2009), MammalDIET (Kissling et al., 2014), AmphiBIO (Oliveira et al., 2017), SeaLifeBase (Palomares & Pauly, 2024), FishBase (Froese & Pauly, 2024), and the traitdata taxonomy table incorporating GBIF Backbone Taxonomy (GBIF Secretariat, 2023; RS-eco, 2023).

text.text: Separate source tables should not be assumed to represent independent observations, and the benchmark was not established as absent from model training or retrieval sources.
Species were matched by normalized genus-species binomials.
Overlapping source variables were retained separately.
Categorical traits were expanded into indicators, keeping species not represented by a source missing.
FishBase indicators coded -1 = yes and0 = no were converted to 1/0.
In the original AmphiBIO processing, unflagged categories among matched species were set to 0.
The source documentation defines such NA entries as unrecorded categories, not verified absence (Oliveira et al., 2017).

text.text: The correlation workflow classified variables by observed values: two distinct nonmissing values were treated as dichotomous; integer columns with three to seven distinct values and range no greater than 7 were treated as polytomous; other numeric columns were treated as continuous.

It then selected Pearson for continuous-continuous pairs, biserial for continuous-dichotomous pairs, polyserial for continuous-polytomous pairs, tetrachoric for dichotomous-dichotomous pairs, and polychoric for two polytomous variables or a polytomous-dichotomous pair (Olsson, 1979; Revelle, 2026).

Constant variables and estimation failures were assigned NA.

text.text: The audit and similarity network used this same species subset.
Claude Opus 4.7 extended, which had not generated the LifeDive values, used its knowledge and web searches to construct a taxonomy-rule comparison and a smaller species-specific spot check.
The report states 7,641 cells in the final rule evaluation and 240 cells in the spot check, while some intermediate and confidence-stratum counts differ.
Section S3 retains the prompt and gives an edited summary with explicit interpretive limits.
Neither procedure was an independent expert adjudication or a uniform probability sample of all cells.

Using the n=200 deeper-validation sub-sample -i.e., from an organism-by-phenotype matrix containing 200 organisms scored across the 196 ordinal phenotype questions -an organism phenotype-similarity network was constructed.
Taxonomic metadata were used to assign organisms to seven plotting groups: Arthropoda, Ascomycota, Chordata, Cnidaria, Mollusca, Tracheophyta, and "Other."
The "Other" category included organisms outside the six focal phyla and was therefore expected to be biologically heterogeneous.
Organism labels were shortened to binomial scientific names for readability, and common names were excluded from node labels to reduce visual crowding.
Pairwise species-profile similarities were computed as polychoric correlations across the 196 questions (Olsson, 1979; Revelle, 2026).
text.formatted: Pairwise species-profile similarities were computed as polychoric correlations across the 196 questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Olsson, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Revelle, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although responses are ordered, questions are heterogeneous and often related to one another; using them as paired observations does not automatically meet the estimator's assumptions.
Shared negative responses and repeated trait content can contribute to high similarity.
The coefficients are therefore treated as descriptive summaries.
Negative correlations were retained in numerical results and set to zero in the plotted edge matrix.
The resulting nonnegative weighted matrix was drawn with qgraph using a force-directed spring layout (Epskamp et al., 2012; Fruchterman & Reingold, 1991).
text.formatted: The resulting nonnegative weighted matrix was drawn with qgraph using a force-directed spring layout <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Epskamp et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fruchterman & Reingold, 1991)</ref>.

Node colors show the phylum-level plotting groups.

Because questions mix biological traits and human-associated descriptions, the graph summarizes the chosen phenotype profiles; it should not be read as a phylogenetic tree or as independent validation of its individual entries.
The completed matrix contains 35,856 species by 196 retained questions, or 7,027,776 entries.
Sampling aimed for family-level breadth and favored accepted names and common names.
The questions span cellular, physiological, anatomical, behavioral, ecological, life-history, and human-salience domains, applying the same response framework across the sampled kingdoms.
Unknown/not applicable and out-of-range responses were treated as missing.
Random-forest classification then completed the retained matrix; 16.6% of its entries were imputed.
The completed matrix supports the reported descriptive analyses but combines original annotations and values predicted from other annotations.
The 14-factor promax-rotated solution was readily interpretable from the displayed pattern coefficients (Table S2).
text.formatted: The 14-factor promax-rotated solution was readily interpretable from the displayed pattern coefficients (Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Assigning each item to the factor on which it had the largest absolute loading yielded the following primary-loading counts: 82 Plant-like items, 12 Fungus-like items, 19 Aquatic items, 15 Insect-like items, 5 Simple items, 10 Robust items, 12 Durable items, 10 Bird-like items, 5 Dangerous items, 5 Shelled items, 5 Drought-tolerant items, 7 Parasitic items, 6 Cold-tolerant items, and 3 Environmentally-sensitive items.
The Plant-like factor was the broadest and strongest dimension.

High positive loadings included cellulose production (.97), etiolation or comparable low-light responses (.96), large fluid-filled vacuoles (.94), mycorrhizal symbiosis (.92), production of fruit or fruiting bodies (.91), phenolic compounds (.91), photosynthesis (.91), boron use (.91), and cell walls (.91).

Strong negative loadings on centrioles (-.94), glycogen storage (-.93), rapid response to mechanical contact (-.92), sodium physiology (-.92), externally acquired vitamins or cofactors (-.85), and motile cells (-.85) reinforced the interpretation that this dimension separates plant-like trait profiles from animal-like or otherwise nonplant physiological profiles.
The Fungus-like factor was also coherent.

Its strongest positive indicators were lignin-degrading enzymes (.93), siderophore production (.84), multinucleate cells (.80), decomposer nutrition (.69), a predominantly haploid life stage (.63), filamentous growth (.58), and extracellular digestion (.58).

Negative loading on multiple distinct tissue types (-.64) further supported the interpretation of this factor as a fungal/decomposer morphology and physiology dimension rather than simply a second plant axis.
The Aquatic factor captured aquatic habitat and physiology.
The strongest positive indicators were survival under water (.86), primarily aquatic habitat (.82), gill or gill-like gas exchange (.82), salinity tolerance (.65), and indeterminate growth (.63).
Negative loadings on periodic shedding of dead mass (-.69), rapid post-fire recovery (-.65), and metabolic heat generation (-.55) helped
Permanent preprint • November 2026 https://www.mooremetrics.com/lifedive/ differentiate the aquatic profile from terrestrial plant regrowth and endothermic animal profiles.
text.formatted: Permanent preprint • November 2026 <ref type="url" target="https://www.mooremetrics.com/lifedive/">mooremetrics.com/lifedive</ref> differentiate the aquatic profile from terrestrial plant regrowth and endothermic animal profiles.

text.text: The Insect-like factor loaded highly on chitin use (.92), chitinase or chitin-degrading enzymes (.69), very small body mass (.65), short lifespan (.64), and specialized surface openings for gas exchange (.62), with strong negative loadings on closed circulatory or vascular systems (-.83), rigid internal skeletons (-.73), and hemoglobin-like physiology (-.73).
These loadings are consistent with an arthropod-like or small invertebrate-like structural dimension.
Several narrower factors represented interpretable ecological or morphological dimensions.

The Simple factor loaded on budding reproduction (.85), gelatinous or jelly-like body composition (.67), and colony or network resource sharing (.46), while negatively loading on intercellular cytoplasmic connections (-.55).

The Robust factor was defined by nuisance or opportunistic ecological status, including being a weed, crop pest, or agricultural nuisance (.89), invasive in some areas (.88), annoying to many humans (.67), urban survival (.61), rapid population growth (.54), and allergenicity (.53).

The Durable factor was marked by hard or durable tissues sought by humans (.75), large body size (.63), protective outer covering (.61), longevity greater than 100 years (.61), fossil-preserving structures (.57), and ecosystem engineering (.46), with negative loadings on hamster-scale smallness (-.59) and fragility (-.49).

The Bird-like factor combined appearance and aerial/reproductive features, including structural coloration (.70), perceived beauty (.68), external eggs/seeds/spores (.59), blue coloration (.56), gliding (.49), orange coloration (.45), and internal gas-filled cavities (.44).
The remaining factors were more compact but substantively clear.
The Dangerous factor loaded on serious threat to human life (.73), venom (.65), defensive toxins (.59), mammalian poison (.57), and ferocity (.46).
The Shelled factor loaded most strongly on calcium carbonate structural material (.78) and tentacles (.71), with additional negative loadings on elongated body form (-.38) and scales (-.34).

The Drought-tolerant factor loaded on long periods without water (.75), arid or desert thriving (.72), survival at 50 degrees Celsius for 100 hours (.64), desiccation and rehydration (.45), and water-storage structures (.40).
The Parasitic factor loaded on parasitism (.76), dependence on close symbiosis (.59), human-body colonization (.41), and living on the surface of another organism (.35).

The Cold-tolerant factor was indicated by polar or Arctic/Antarctic occurrence (.56), freezing tolerance (.47), seasonal long-distance movement (.45), and temperature-triggered developmental transitions (.31), with a negative loading on tropical occurrence (-.59).
The Environmentally-sensitive factor loaded on sensitivity to pollution or environmental change (.76), endangered status (.64), and freshwater habitat (.62).
Overall, the solution recovered broad biological dimensions that are plausible across kingdoms while also identifying narrower, interpretable ecological and structural trait clusters.

text.text: The factor-score scatterplots provided an intuitive check on the interpretability of selected dimensions (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The factor-score scatterplots provided an intuitive check on the interpretability of selected dimensions (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In the Durable versus Plant-like panel, woody plants occupied the high Plant-like and high Durable region: English oak and coast redwood had among the highest scores on both dimensions.

Other plants, such as sunflower, Eurasian dandelion, fragrant water-lily, bracken fern, and common haircap moss, also scored high on Plant-like but lower on Durable, consistent with their nonwoody or less massive forms.
Most animals had negative Plant-like scores.

Large or structurally robust animals and animal-like taxa, including American alligator, African bush elephant, American lobster, polar bear, Pacific green sea turtle, humpback whale, and staghorn coral, occupied higher positions on Durable than smaller or more delicate organisms such as moon jellyfish, housefly, monarch butterfly, and European squid.
Fungal examples tended to cluster at positive Plant-like but low Durable scores, reflecting shared nonanimal properties without wood-like durability.
The Aquatic versus Dangerous panel similarly separated familiar trait profiles.

Fish and marine organisms, including Atlantic cod, Atlantic salmon, goldfish, common clownfish, short-snouted seahorse, blue crab, European squid, bay mussel, staghorn coral, giant plumed anemone, and moon jellyfish, had high Aquatic scores.

Venomous or predatory organisms such as southern black widow, largeclawed scorpion, Bermuda centipede, king cobra, tiger, lion, goliath birdeater, gray wolf, polar bear, and common vampire bat had high Dangerous scores and generally lower Aquatic scores.
The great white shark occupied the high-Aquatic/high-Dangerous region, demonstrating that the factors can jointly represent organisms that combine aquatic life with high hazard.
Conversely, aquatic but comparatively low-danger organisms such as common bottlenose dolphin and humpback whale were located away from the high-Dangerous cluster.
The plotted examples illustrate the relative profiles, but they are not a held-out validation.
In particular, dolphins and whales have Aquatic scores near zero, so that axis cannot be interpreted as a direct habitat classifier.
Table S3 reports the five largest absolute item correlations for each of 44 selected criteria.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> reports the five largest absolute item correlations for each of 44 selected criteria.

text.text: These cover taxonomy and selected ecological traits from EltonTraits, PanTHERIA, MammalDIET, AmphiBIO, and SeaLifeBase.

Broad taxonomic indicators often have large associations with recognizable trait contrasts: Animalia with cellulose (-0.99), cell walls (-0.97), and centrioles (0.98); Plantae with cellulose (0.99), photosynthesis (0.97), and cell walls (0.97); and Mammalia with hair, fur, or trichomes (0.99).
The mammal indicator is negatively associated (-0.98) with the question about seeds, eggs outside the body, or spores.
The qualifier "outside the body" is material to interpreting this item.
These are selected latent-correlation estimates, not percentages of correctly classified cells.

Among selected within-taxon comparisons, nighttime activity correlated with bird nocturnality at 0.92, with the EltonTraits mammal-nocturnality indicator at 0.75, and with the corresponding diurnal indicator at -0.73.
Marine-mammal foraging correlated with underwater survival at 0.97.
A mammal-eats-mammals indicator correlated with prey capture at 0.59, perceived ferocity at 0.58, and black coloration at 0.55; the last is less directly interpretable.
Marine-invertebrate sessility correlated with the sessile-life item at 0.84.
AmphiBIO-derived associations remain visible in Table S3 but are excluded from affirmative presence/absence validation because of their source-coding uncertainty.

Examples include lignin-degradation items among birds or mammals and a genus-age item associated with marine

text.text: Sparse cross-tabulations, boundary estimates, annotation mistakes, criterion coding, and selection of extrema may all contribute; the retained results do not isolate a single cause.
The appropriate conclusion is that selected associations recover recognizable contrasts alongside problematic matches, rather than that every large coefficient validates a trait.
The network recovered a strong phylum-level signal.
Mean within-phylum polychoric correlations were high for Ascomycota (mean ρ = .877), Cnidaria (ρ = .853), Arthropoda (ρ = .823), Chordata (ρ = .810), Mollusca (ρ = .785), and Tracheophyta (ρ = .766).

In contrast, the "Other" category had a much lower mean within-group correlation (ρ = .510), consistent with its composition as a residual group containing algae, bryophytes, nematodes, sponges, echinoderms, annelids, and other non-focal lineages.
The strongest between-phylum similarities were among animal groups, particularly Chordata-Arthropoda (mean ρ = .689), Chordata-Mollusca (ρ = .680), and Arthropoda-Mollusca (ρ = .668).

Tracheophytes were much less similar to animal groups, including Chordata (ρ = .171), Arthropoda (ρ = .233), and Mollusca (ρ = .205), explaining the visual separation of the plant cluster from the animal-dominated portion of the network.
At the organism level, the strongest positive correlations were generally interpretable as either close taxonomic similarity or broad functional similarity.

Examples of very strong associations occurred among trees: jackfruit, Artocarpus heterophyllus, and camphor tree, Cinnamomum camphora (ρ = .997); jackfruit and bald cypress, Taxodium distichum (ρ = .989); and camphor tree and bald cypress (ρ = .985).

Other strong positive examples included frog-frog similarity between Boulenger's callulops frog, Callulops robustus, and the San Lorenzo robber frog, Serranobatrachus megalops (ρ = .974); flatfish similarity between the threespot sand flounder, Ancylopsetta dendritica, and the patchtail tonguefish, Symphurus rhytisma (ρ = .973); reef-fish similarity between the yellowtail tubelip wrasse, Labropsis xanthura, and the network reefgoby, Priolepis agrena (ρ = .972); and sea-anemone similarity between Acricoactis brachyacontis and Phelliactis robusta (ρ = .967).
The strongest negative correlations were much weaker in magnitude and were not displayed in the graph because negative values were set to zero prior to plotting.

Examples included jackfruit and the loricariid catfish Loricaria cuffyi (ρ = -.164), jackfruit and the glass knifefish Japigny kirschbaum (ρ = -.116), and common lake sedge, Carex lacustris, and the Haitian solenodon, Solenodon paradoxus (ρ = -.115).
The positions of the major clusters are biologically plausible.

Tracheophytes formed a dense and spatially distinct cluster, consistent with the shared plant functional traits represented in the phenotype set, such as photosynthesis, cell walls, cellulose-rich and lignified tissues, perennial growth, vascular or structural support, seeds, secondary compounds, and plant-specific ecological interactions.

Plant functional traits are commonly interpreted as integrated morphological, physiological, and phenological features that reflect ecological strategy, which helps explain why functionally similar plants can cluster together even when they are not close relatives (Pérez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Plant functional traits are commonly interpreted as integrated morphological, physiological, and phenological features that reflect ecological strategy, which helps explain why functionally similar plants can cluster together even when they are not close relatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pérez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The animal groups occupied the opposite side of the network.

Chordates and arthropods were adjacent because both groups include many active, bilaterally organized animals with complex sensory responses, external or internal support structures, motility, feeding on other organisms, and egg-or gamete-based reproduction.

Molluscs occupied a boundary region between chordates, arthropods, and cnidarians, which is also reasonable: the molluscan sample includes active cephalopods, terrestrial gastropods, marine bivalves, limpets, and other forms that share
Permanent preprint • November 2026 https://www.mooremetrics.com/lifedive/ different subsets of traits with different animal groups.
text.formatted: Permanent preprint • November 2026 <ref type="url" target="https://www.mooremetrics.com/lifedive/">mooremetrics.com/lifedive</ref> different subsets of traits with different animal groups.

text.text: Cnidarians clustered near other aquatic invertebrates, reflecting traits such as radial organization, tentacles, sessility or limited adult movement in many taxa, gelatinous or colonial forms, and calcium-carbonate-associated structures in some species.
Several boundary placements were especially informative.
The mollusc Acanthosepion ellipticum, a cuttlefish, was positioned near chordates rather than deeply within the molluscan region.
This is biologically sensible in a phenotype network.

Cuttlefishes are cephalopod molluscs, but cephalopods are active marine predators with sophisticated sensory systems and behavioral flexibility; in broad phenotype space, an active, visually oriented, predatory, bilaterian, swimming cuttlefish can resemble fishes more than it resembles slow terrestrial snails or sessile bivalves (Villanueva et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Cuttlefishes are cephalopod molluscs, but cephalopods are active marine predators with sophisticated sensory systems and behavioral flexibility; in broad phenotype space, an active, visually oriented, predatory, bilaterian, swimming cuttlefish can resemble fishes more than it resembles slow terrestrial snails or sessile bivalves <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Villanueva et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The correlations support this interpretation: Acanthosepion ellipticum correlated strongly with multiple chordate fishes, including Gross's dragonet, Callionymus grossi (ρ = .866), the common silver-biddy, Gerres subfasciatus (ρ = .842), Englert's scorpionfish, Scorpaenodes englerti (ρ = .836), and the freetail brotula, Bidenichthys capensis (ρ = .833).
By contrast, the mollusc Discus catskillensis, the angular disc land snail, fell closer to arthropods.
This placement is also plausible.

Discus catskillensis is a small terrestrial gastropod with a protective shell, and in the phenotype matrix it shares a "small terrestrial invertebrate" syndrome with many arthropods: small body size, external protective structures, egg production, terrestrial microhabitat use, vulnerability to desiccation and predation, and relatively limited locomotion compared with vertebrates.

Its strongest correlations still included other molluscs, such as the tawny glass snail Euconulus fulvus (ρ = .913) and the bicolor cactussnail Xerarionta tryoni (ρ = .876), but it also correlated strongly with arthropods, including the oribatid mite Bipassalozetes macedonicus (ρ = .821) and the mite Asternolaelaps fecundus (ρ = .802).
Thus, its position reflects phenotypic overlap between terrestrial gastropods and small arthropods rather than a taxonomic ambiguity.
The exceptionally strong links among jackfruit, camphor tree, and bald cypress are also interpretable, but they illustrate an important distinction between phenotypic and phylogenetic similarity.
Jackfruit is a tropical angiosperm tree in Moraceae, camphor tree is an aromatic evergreen tree in Lauraceae, and bald cypress is a long-lived deciduous conifer.

These taxa are not close phylogenetic relatives; however, all are large, perennial, woody, seed-producing plants with substantial standing biomass, durable structural tissues, long life spans, secondary chemistry, and human-recognized uses or cultivation histories.
These shared functional and architectural traits can generate very high phenotype correlations even across deep plant lineages (Lee et al., 2022; Ranasinghe et al., 2019; Wilhite & Toliver, 1990).
text.formatted: These shared functional and architectural traits can generate very high phenotype correlations even across deep plant lineages <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lee et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ranasinghe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Wilhite & Toliver, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the strong bonds among these three trees are biologically plausible as functional-trait similarities, but they should not be interpreted as evidence of close evolutionary relationship.
The "Other" nodes generally occupied biologically interpretable positions rather than forming a coherent cluster.
Gloeochaete wittrockiana, a glaucophyte alga, was positioned near Ascomycota.

This placement makes sense only in phenotype-space terms: Gloeochaete is not a fungus, but as a small, cell-walled, non-animal, aquatic/microbial photosynthetic eukaryote it shares some coarse traits with fungi and other non-animal organisms.
Its strongest correlation was with the green alga Pteromonas aculeata (ρ = .853), followed by more moderate relationships with fungi and plant-like organisms.
Thus, proximity to Ascomycota reflects overlapping non-animal phenotype states, not fungal identity (Jackson & Reyes-Prieto, 2014).
text.formatted: Thus, proximity to Ascomycota reflects overlapping non-animal phenotype states, not fungal identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jackson & Reyes-Prieto, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The bryophytes Lorentziella imbricata and Tortula muralis were located near Tracheophyta, which is one of the clearest biologically expected placements among the "Other" nodes.

Bryophytes are nonvascular land plants, whereas tracheophytes are vascular land plants; despite major differences in vascular tissue, sporophyte dominance, and body architecture, they share many land-plant traits, including photosynthesis, cell walls, spores or gametes, terrestrial growth, and responses to water and light.

Lorentziella imbricata correlated strongly with the wall screw-moss Tortula muralis (ρ = .843) and with several tracheophytes, including Mohr's thoroughwort, Eupatorium mohrii (ρ = .838), and Rydberg's spring-beauty, Claytonia multiscapa (ρ = .835).
Tortula muralis showed a similar pattern, correlating strongly with the moss Homalothecium nevadense (ρ = .890), Lorentziella imbricata (ρ = .843), and several tracheophytes.
This supports the interpretation that "Other" is a plotting category, not a biological group (Harris et al., 2022; Larraín et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This supports the interpretation that "Other" is a plotting category, not a biological group <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Harris et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Larraín et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The nematode Geomonhystera mexiquense was located near arthropods, and this is also biologically plausible.
Nematodes and arthropods are not the same phylum, but both belong to the molting-animal clade Ecdysozoa, and the phenotype set captures broad features of small bilaterian invertebrates.

Geomonhystera mexiquense correlated most strongly with arthropods, including the mite Lophonotacarus minutus (ρ = .911), the bush-cricket Isophya ciucasi (ρ = .874), the mite Asternolaelaps fecundus (ρ = .868), and the mite Hemipteroseius ageneius (ρ = .861).
Thus, its position near arthropods is one of the more biologically coherent "Other" placements (Aguinaldo et al., 1997; Cid del Prado-Vera et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Thus, its position near arthropods is one of the more biologically coherent "Other" placements <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aguinaldo et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cid del Prado-Vera et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, Pteromonas aculeata occupied a central, weakly assigned position.

This is consistent with its biology as a green alga: it shares photosynthetic and cell-wall traits with plants and other algae, but lacks vascular tissue, woody architecture, seeds, and most macroscopic tracheophyte traits.

At the same time, its small size, aquatic habit, motile-cell features, and microbial-like body organization distinguish it from most land plants and allow moderate similarity to several non-plant groups.
Its group-level affinities were diffuse rather than concentrated, with mean correlations ranging from ρ = .358 to ρ = .498 across the plotted phylum categories.
The strongest organism-level association was with Gloeochaete wittrockiana (ρ = .853), another algal "Other" taxon.
Therefore, its central location is best interpreted as a mixed-trait or bridging position, not as membership in any of the focal phylum clusters.
The network organizes many broad trait profiles in recognizable ways, including woody plants, fungi, vertebrates, and several invertebrate groups.
These interpretations are descriptive and often post hoc.
Apparent agreement with taxonomy can partly follow from questions about taxonomically characteristic properties and shared absences.
Negative correlations were omitted from the plotted edge matrix, and spring-layout distance is not a calibrated evolutionary or functional distance.

text.text: This section is an edited account of the audit performed by Claude Opus 4.7 extended.
The prompt is reproduced below.
Repeated activity messages and unsupported extrapolations from the original response have been omitted.
The numerical results remain those reported by the auditing model; the cell-level evaluation has not been rerun for this preprint.
Agreement with the model-generated reference judgments should not be equated with independently adjudicated biological accuracy.
I have a large table of animal, plant, and fungus characteristics that I've obtained using Grok's batch API.
I now want to get an idea of how accurate these characteristics are.

Each characteristic is in the form of a question, and the possible response options are:0 = Definitely No1 = Probably No2 = Unknown (or not applicable)3 = Probably Yes4 = Definitely Yes I've selected a random sample of 200 of these organisms (out of over 35,000) and am attaching their data.
I would like you to do the absolute best you can, given your existing knowledge and all tools available to you, to check what percentage of these responses are correct.
Use whatever approach you think will yield the most useful approximation of accuracy.
The audit started with 200 species by 196 questions, totaling 39,200 cells.
For the taxonomy-rule comparison, the auditing model assigned broad organism groups and selected approximately 50 questions for which it expected broad taxonomic rules to be informative.
It compared codes 0/1 with expected No and codes 3/4 with expected Yes.
The model revised some rules and taxonomic assignments after examining disagreements, so the reference rules were not fixed independently of the observed data.
This can correct mistaken reference judgments, but it can also make the resulting agreement optimistic.
For the species-specific check, the model selected 20 organisms and 12 questions per organism and used its knowledge and targeted searches where it lacked confidence.

The report names sources such as IUCN, Animal Diversity Web, BirdLife, taxonomic literature, and Wikipedia, but does not supply a complete cell-by-cell source and adjudication ledger in the manuscript.
It is therefore more accurate to call this a model-assisted spot check than a fully independently web-verified evaluation of all 240 cells.
Selected taxonomy-rule comparison 7,641 in final summary 96.5%
Selected species-specific spot check 240 Approximately 237/240 (98.8%)
The rule-based rate is reported as 96.5% for a final total of 7,641 evaluable cells (about 19.5% of the 39,200-cell matrix).
The spot-check result is approximately 237/240, or 98.8%.
The questions were selected, the smaller species sample was purposive, and the reference labels were fallible model judgments.
Neither result can be extrapolated to the full LifeDive matrix.
No

The response counts sum to 39,200.
Extreme substantive codes (0 and 4) account for 34,029 cells (86.8%), and intermediate substantive codes (1 and 3) for 5,171 (13.2%).
These percentages describe the entire audited matrix, not the smaller rule-evaluable subset.
The lack of code 2 in this matrix cannot establish the raw annotation model's abstention rate.
Preprocessing and imputation can remove Unknown responses, and the audit report does not resolve the provenance of each examined cell.
Within the separate taxonomy-rule subset, the original report gives 97.1% agreement for 7,440 extreme-code cells and 73.4% for 203 intermediate-code cells.
These counts total 7,643, whereas the final total is 7,641; an intermediate stage of the transcript also used 7,643.
The discrepancy cannot be resolved from the summary.
These strata are retained here as approximate reported outputs, not as calibrated probabilities or as a basis for weighting the entire dataset.
Even reconciled category differences would show confidence ordering, not full probabilistic calibration.
The following subgroup summaries are reproduced from the audit.
The groups shown are selected groups, not an exhaustive partition of all 200 species.
These are the auditing model's reported group assignments and counts; group membership was not reconciled with the taxonomy in Table S1.

Group Species Evaluated cells Reported agreement Bony fish 28 1,288 97.0% Insects 26 988 98.2% Angiosperms 30 810 93.6% Birds 14 700 97.0% Reptiles 14 616 96.4% Mammals 11 517 97.7% Permanent preprint • November 2026 mooremetrics.com/lifedive Group Species Evaluated cells Reported agreement Arachnids 10 410 95.4% Fungi 10 340 96.5% Amphibians 6 270 96.3% Gastropod mollusks 7 259 98.5% Cnidarians 6 234 95.3% Crustaceans 4 144 99.3% The report identified the following lower-agreement questions.
Their wording is abbreviated here; identifiers are those used in the audit and are not the row order of the sorted pattern table.
Because taxonomic rules may omit species exceptions or qualifiers in the actual question, disagreement can reflect a mistaken reference rule as well as an annotation error.

Audit Q Question (abbreviated) Reported agreement 190 Structures commonly preserved in fossil record 78.5% 75 Has scales or squama 83.3% 53 Alternation of multicellular haploid/diploid generations 88.7% 26 Can survive long periods underwater 89.2% 157 Primarily aquatic 90.4% 195 Specialized gas-exchange pores (stomata/spiracles/lenticels) 91.8% 165 Uses hemoglobin or hemoglobin-like molecules 93.5%
The original report itself documents errors in the auditor's organism classification and notes that some initial rules were too rigid.
In addition, its summary rule for reproduction omitted the phrase "eggs (outside the body)" from the actual item, which matters for interpreting mammalian responses.
A cycad was also invoked in a discussion of angiosperm errors even though it is a gymnosperm.
These examples show why model-generated reference standards need explicit, independently checked definitions.
The audit supports a limited conclusion: high agreement was reported for particular selected cells, and some ambiguous questions and questionable annotations were identified for review.
It does not establish overall 95-97% accuracy, the number of correct entries in the full dataset, or the effectiveness of re-prompting.

A stronger evaluation would use a prespecified sample across species and questions, separate generated from imputed values, retain source citations and explicit negative evidence, adjudicate disagreements with relevant expertise, and report uncertainty that respects the sampling and clustering structure.
